note: EXAMPLE / TEMPLATE. Copy to standards.json and adapt: narrow each `paths` to your source root, drop framework-specific entries you don't use (their label says so), and add your own. A standard = an idea with a detector. Detectors come in two layers. FLOOR = `ast`/`grep` detectors, auto-scanned by scan_coverage.py: cheap, precise, always-on. CEILING = `kind: manual` standards the scan skips on purpose: judgment-heavy rules that no AST pattern captures, recorded here so the declared baseline is COMPLETE, and owned by code review / the role-based review-avatar lane. Dimensions in use: security, resilience, observability, privacy, cost, quality. ACTIVATION (ADR 0020): every standard carries an `activation` of `{baseline:true}` (always in scope) or `{rungs:[{min_maturity,min_stakes,...}]}` (in scope only when the project's declared maturity x stakes meet a rung). Maturity ladder prototype<first-users<production; stakes ladder internal<external<public-adversarial. The baseline = Sanity (DRY/consistency) + the cheap common-sense safety rung; depth-laddered standards add heavier rungs gated to higher maturity AND stakes. See ../knowledge/detector-model.md for the detector model and the project-state surface.

ideas.label: External DB connections must have error handling
ideas.statement: Code that opens a connection to an external database must do so inside exception handling, so an unreachable host or bad credential surfaces as an actionable failure rather than an unhandled traceback.

solves: an external DB being down or misconfigured crashes the request with a raw traceback
contract.applies_when: code opens a connection to an external database

ideas.label: Outbound HTTP requests must set a timeout
ideas.statement: Every outbound requests.* call must pass an explicit timeout, so a hung or slow remote host cannot block a worker or request indefinitely.

solves: a hung remote host blocks a worker or request forever when no timeout is set
improves: resilience of every outbound HTTP integration
contract.applies_when: code makes an outbound HTTP call via the requests library

ideas.label: Blocking subprocess calls must set a timeout
ideas.statement: A blocking subprocess.run/check_output/check_call/call must pass a timeout so a wedged child process cannot hang a worker forever.

solves: a child process that never returns hangs the calling worker indefinitely

ideas.label: Dynamic code execution (eval/exec) must be reviewed and sandboxed
ideas.statement: eval()/exec() turn data into code; every call is a code-injection surface and must be deliberately reviewed, fed only trusted input, and ideally run in a restricted namespace. Treat each hit as 'prove this is safe', not 'this is a bug'.

solves: attacker-influenced data reaching eval/exec becomes remote code execution
improves: auditability of every dynamic-execution site in the tree

ideas.label: subprocess must not use shell=True
ideas.statement: shell=True runs the command through a shell, so any interpolated value becomes a shell-injection vector. Pass an argument list instead.

solves: interpolating a value into a shell=True command line enables command injection
contract.applies_when: code invokes a subprocess with shell=True

ideas.label: TLS verification must not be disabled
ideas.statement: verify=False on an outbound request disables certificate validation and exposes the call to man-in-the-middle interception. Fix the trust store instead of disabling verification.

solves: a verify=False call can be silently MITM'd, leaking credentials or data
contract.applies_when: code makes an outbound TLS request with verification disabled

ideas.label: Secrets must not be hardcoded in source
ideas.statement: API keys, passwords, and tokens must come from the environment or a secret store, never a literal in source — a committed secret lives in git history forever. (grep heuristic; review each hit, config(...)/os.environ reads are fine.)

solves: a secret committed to source leaks through the repo and its history permanently
contract.applies_when: a secret-looking name is assigned a string literal

ideas.label: Template autoescaping must not be bypassed on dynamic data [Django/Jinja-specific]
ideas.statement: mark_safe()/|safe disables HTML autoescaping; on any user- or external-derived value that is a stored/reflected XSS vector. Every use must be reviewed to confirm the content is static or already sanitized. Drop this standard if your stack has no template autoescaping.

solves: marking attacker-influenced content safe renders it unescaped, enabling XSS

ideas.label: Long-running service code must log, not print
ideas.statement: Application/service/worker code must emit through the structured logger, not print(), so output is captured, leveled, timestamped, and correlatable in production. (Narrow `paths` to your long-running code; print() is fine in CLI entrypoints and scripts.)

solves: print() output is uncaptured, unleveled, and invisible in production logs

ideas.label: Endpoints must authorize the caller against the specific object, not just authenticate
ideas.statement: Any endpoint that loads a record by an id from the request must check that the caller is permitted to access THAT object — not merely that they are logged in. Authentication answers 'who are you'; authorization answers 'may you touch this row'. Missing object-level checks are broken access control (IDOR), the most common real-world web vulnerability. Owned by code review / the Attacker review-avatar — not mechanically detectable here.

solves: a logged-in user reads or mutates another tenant's object by changing an id in the URL
improves: access-control correctness on every object-scoped endpoint
contract.applies_when: an endpoint loads a record using an id taken from the request

ideas.label: Secrets and PII must not enter logs or LLM prompts
ideas.statement: Credentials and personal data must never be written to logs, error responses, or LLM prompt payloads. Logs get shipped to third-party aggregators; prompts get sent to model providers and may be retained. Owned by code review / the Privacy review-avatar — not mechanically detectable here.

solves: secrets/PII leak through log aggregators or model-provider prompt retention
improves: data-handling posture of logging and AI integrations
contract.applies_when: code logs, returns errors, or builds an LLM prompt from values that may contain secrets or PII

ideas.label: Endpoints that trigger expensive work must be abuse-bounded
ideas.statement: Any endpoint that kicks off a crawl, an LLM/AI call, a bulk export, or other metered/expensive work must be guarded against runaway spend. The COMMON-SENSE rung (baseline floor): require authentication and a basic per-caller quota / sanity bound so a single caller cannot trivially run up unbounded cost. The HARDENED rung (production + public-adversarial): real rate-limiting and cost-DoS / abuse-resistance infrastructure (token buckets, per-tenant budgets, anomaly throttling). A low-stakes internal tool stops at the common-sense floor; do not gold-plate DDoS infrastructure onto it. Owned by code review / the Operator and Attacker review-avatars — not mechanically detectable here.

solves: an under-bounded endpoint lets a caller drive unbounded compute, API, or model spend
improves: cost safety and abuse resistance of expensive operations
contract.applies_when: an endpoint triggers metered, billed, or otherwise expensive work

ideas.label: External content and LLM output must be contained at the trust boundary
ideas.statement: Content from outside the trust boundary — crawled/third-party HTML, uploaded files, and LLM output — must be contained before it crosses INTO a prompt, generated code, persistent storage, or rendered output. The COMMON-SENSE rung (baseline floor): structural prompt delimiters, parse-and-validate, a never-obey-crawled-content rule, escape/sanitize on render — cheap, no reason not to from day one. The HARDENED rung (production + public-adversarial): a second model pre-screening all incoming text for prompt-injection / safety, sandboxed execution of any generated code, and threat-modeled content quarantine. Stakes selects the rung: a low-stakes internal tool's appropriate ceiling is the common-sense floor. Owned by code review / the Attacker review-avatar — not mechanically detectable here.

solves: hostile external content or manipulated LLM output crosses unchecked into code, storage, prompts, or the page
improves: integrity of every trust-boundary crossing in AI and crawl pipelines
contract.applies_when: external content or LLM output flows into a prompt, generated code, storage, or rendered output

ideas.label: A second model must pre-screen all incoming text for prompt-injection / safety [high-stakes rung only]
ideas.statement: Run every piece of externally-sourced text (crawled HTML, uploads, user messages) through an independent safety/prompt-injection screening model BEFORE it reaches the primary LLM or any code-generation path. This is the heavy end of the prompt-injection depth ladder — it adds a second model call to every input and is justified ONLY for a production, public-adversarial service. It is explicitly NOT required for a low-stakes internal tool, whose appropriate ceiling is the common-sense delimiter/validate rung of idea-untrusted-content-boundary. Owned by code review / the Attacker review-avatar — not mechanically detectable here.

solves: a sophisticated indirect prompt-injection slips past structural delimiters into the primary model
improves: adversarial robustness of the AI input boundary for a public, high-stakes service
contract.applies_when: a production, public-adversarial service feeds externally-sourced text to an LLM or code-generation path

ideas.label: Key user workflows must emit product-analytics signal
ideas.statement: A workflow you cannot measure is a workflow you cannot improve. Key multi-step user journeys must emit product-analytics events (step entry/exit, success, failure, abandonment, time-on-step) so friction and feature adoption are measured from real usage, not guessed. The user-facing complement to application logging. Owned by product/design review / the Naive-User review-avatar — not mechanically detectable here.

solves: friction, drop-off, and dead features stay invisible because no usage signal is emitted
improves: the team's understanding of how users actually move through the product
contract.applies_when: a user-facing multi-step workflow ships without usage instrumentation
